Student AI Agreement
1. Use AI to learn, not replace thinking.
2. Be honest about my work and follow teacher directions.
3. Verify important information before trusting it.
4. Ask better questions and use AI to deepen understanding.
Part I — Understanding AI
This part introduces the foundation students need before using AI more actively: what
artificial intelligence is, how it works at a basic level, and why understanding it matters
for learning, school, and everyday life.
Chapter 1 — Understanding Artificial Intelligence
Key Question
What is artificial intelligence, and why does it matter for students today?
Learning Objectives
 Understand what artificial intelligence is in simple terms
What Is Artificial Intelligence?
Artificial intelligence, often shortened to AI, refers to computer systems designed to
perform tasks that usually require human intelligence. These tasks include understanding
language, identifying patterns, generating responses, solving problems, and making
predictions.
AI as a Tool for Thinking
The most important idea in this chapter is that AI should be understood as a tool for
thinking, not a shortcut for avoiding thought. There is a major difference between a
student who uses AI to deepen understanding and a student who uses AI only to
complete work faster.
Try This
Prompt Example
Explain artificial intelligence in a way a high school student would understand.
Prompt Example
Give me three examples of how students might use AI for learning.
Chapter Summary
In this chapter, you explored the basic idea of artificial intelligence and why it matters
for students. The most important takeaway is simple: AI is most valuable when it
supports human thinking rather than replaces it.
Chapter 2 — How AI Actually Works
Key Question
How do artificial intelligence systems generate responses, and why do they sometimes
make mistakes?
Learning Objectives
Training AI Systems
Artificial intelligence systems do not begin with human-like understanding. They are
built and trained using enormous amounts of data.
This training data may include books, articles, websites, research papers, conversations,
and many other forms of written language. During training, the AI system examines
Prediction, Not Understanding
AI generates responses by prediction, not by understanding.
When you type a prompt into an AI system, it does not pause and think like a person
would. It does not reflect on its own experiences or reason through the meaning in the
same way a human mind does. Instead, it predicts what words are most likely to come
AI Is Not a Search Engine
Many students compare AI tools to search engines, but the two are not the same.  A
search engine usually finds existing information and links you to sources. An AI tool
generates a brand-new response based on patterns in data. That makes AI feel more
conversational, but it also means you must be more careful.  When you use a search

Chapter 3 — AI as a Learning Partner
Key Question
How can students use artificial intelligence to support learning instead of simply getting
answers?
Learning Objectives
The Difference Between Answers and Understanding
There is a big difference between receiving an answer and actually understanding
something. Imagine two students preparing for a science quiz. The first student asks AI
for the definition of photosynthesis, reads the result, and moves on. The second asks for
the concept to be explained in simple terms, followed by an example and a quiz
This is why AI works best when it does more than explain. It should also help students
rehearse, test, revise, and strengthen knowledge.
For example, after receiving an explanation of the water cycle, a student could ask:
Create five quiz questions about the water cycle.

What makes AI different is that it can support a more interactive kind of learning.

Part II — Learning to Prompt and Think with AI
This part focuses on one of the most important student AI skills: asking better
questions. It helps students learn how prompting, inquiry, and critical thinking shape the
quality of AI support they receive.
Chapter 4 — The Power of Good Prompts
Key Question
How does the way you ask a question affect the quality of an AI response?
Learning Objectives
 Understand what a prompt is
The Prompt Pyramid
A helpful way to think about prompting is to imagine a pyramid. At the bottom are very
simple prompts. As you move upward, prompts become more powerful because they
include more structure and more useful detail.
Basic prompt: “Explain the water cycle.” Better prompt: “Explain the water cycle step
How Students Can Improve Their Prompts
You do not need to write the perfect prompt on your first try. Strong AI users often
improve prompts as they go. A student might begin with a basic question, realize the
answer is too broad, and ask again with more detail. That is not failure. It is refinement.

Chapter 5 — AI for Research and Critical
Thinking
Key Question
How can students use AI to support research while still thinking critically and verifying
information?
Using AI to Start Research
One of the best uses of AI in research is at the beginning of the process, when students
need help understanding the big picture. For example, a student beginning a project on
the Industrial Revolution might ask for an overview of the topic and why it changed
society. A prompt like that can help the student identify major themes before moving
This is also where AI can make learning feel more interactive. It can help students
explore ideas that might otherwise feel abstract or one-sided.
The AI Time Machine
One especially engaging research strategy is to use AI to simulate historical or
perspective-based interviews.
Students should confirm important information using:
 textbooks
 teacher materials
 library resources
 academic databases

Teachers can use AI as part of a research literacy lesson by asking students to compare
an AI-generated explanation with textbook or source-based material.

Part III — AI for School Success
This part focuses on the everyday ways students can use AI to become more effective
learners. It brings AI into the practical realities of school by showing how it can support
studying, writing, problem solving, coding, creativity, and organization without replacing
independent thinking.
Chapter 6 — AI for Studying Smarter
Key Question
How can AI help students study more effectively and remember what they learn?
Learning Objectives
 Understand how AI can support active studying
Turning AI Into a Study Coach
AI becomes most useful for studying when students treat it like a partner in the review
process. A student preparing for a biology test, for example, might ask the tool to create
ten quiz questions about the cell cycle and then explain which answers were wrong and
why. That sequence turns AI from a passive information source into an active study
Quiz me on chemical reactions one question at a time.
Because AI can respond dynamically, students can keep going, ask follow-up questions,
and request harder or easier questions depending on how confident they feel.
This makes studying more flexible and more interactive than simply reading a review
sheet.
A student might begin by asking for a short explanation of mitosis. Then they might ask
for five quiz questions. After missing two of them, they could ask for a simpler
explanation of those specific ideas. Finally, they could request a second quiz to see
whether they improved.
That process is much stronger than reading the same notes over and over.
might ask the tool to turn notes into a study guide with key terms and definitions, then
use that guide as the basis for practice questions or self-testing.
For example, students can ask AI to:
 summarize a chapter
 turn notes into flashcards

Teachers can use AI as a study support tool by asking students to compare study
methods.
For example, one group could review a topic by rereading notes, while another group
uses AI to generate questions and explain mistakes. Students can then reflect on which
Chapter 7 — AI for Writing, Revision, and
Communication
Key Question
How can students use AI to support writing, revision, and communication without
losing their own voice and ideas?
AI as a Brainstorming Partner
One of the hardest parts of writing is simply getting started.
Students may know the general topic of an assignment but still feel uncertain about what
angle to take, what claim to make, or what ideas are worth developing. In those
moments, AI can act like a brainstorming partner.
The response may provide a basic structure:
 introduction
 main claim
 supporting points
 counterargument
Protecting Student Voice
Student writing should still sound like the student.
This is one of the most important rules in this chapter.
A strong essay is not just correct. It reflects the student’s thinking, word choice, and
interpretation. If AI rewrites too much, the work may begin to sound polished but
Used this way, AI supports revision and communication. It does not replace the writer’s
judgment.
Writing Across School Subjects
One useful thing about AI-supported writing is that it can help students communicate
clearly in many different classes.
Classroom Idea
Teachers can use AI in writing instruction by asking students to compare human writing
choices with AI-generated suggestions.
For example, students might write a short paragraph and then ask AI for three revision
suggestions. The class can then discuss:

Chapter 8 — AI for Problem Solving
Key Question
How can students use AI to solve problems more effectively without depending on it
for every answer?
Learning Objectives
Why Problem Solving Feels Hard
Many school problems are difficult not because the topic is impossible, but because the
path is unclear.
A student may know the formula for slope, understand the definition of velocity, or
remember the parts of an equation, but still feel stuck when facing an unfamiliar
These are strong uses of AI because they keep the student focused on understanding the
reasoning.
Using AI to Recognize Patterns
One of the most important parts of problem solving is pattern recognition.
Students become stronger problem solvers when they begin to notice that many
Students can also ask:
 What is the first thing I should notice in this problem?
 Why is this formula the right one to use?
 Where do students usually make mistakes here?
 Can you give me one easier example and one harder example?

A student named Marcus is working on a quadratic equation in algebra. He remembers
seeing similar problems in class, but he is not sure how to begin.
He asks AI:
Show me how to solve this quadratic equation step by step and explain why each step

Chapter 9 — AI for Coding Help
Key Question
How can students use AI to learn coding more effectively without becoming dependent
on it?
Learning Objectives
Why Coding Feels Different From Other Subjects
Coding is different from many other school tasks because students are not just learning
facts. They are learning a system.
To write code successfully, students need to understand:
 how instructions are structured
Using AI to Debug Errors
Another major use of AI in coding is debugging.
Debugging means identifying and fixing problems in code. This is a normal part of
programming. In fact, learning to debug is one of the most important programming
skills students can develop.
This kind of back-and-forth can make coding feel much more manageable, especially for
beginners.
It also reinforces an important habit: coding is a process of building, testing, revising,
and improving.
The Risk of Overdependence
 explaining which part to build first
 helping fix errors along the way
A student might ask:
Help me build a simple number guessing game in Python, one step at a time.
That is a strong prompt because it asks for guided development rather than a finished

Chapter 10 — AI for Creativity and Brainstorming
Key Question
How can students use AI to generate ideas and explore creativity without letting the tool
take over the creative process?
Learning Objectives
Why Brainstorming Matters
Many students struggle most at the beginning of a project.
They may be assigned a topic but have no idea what angle to take. They may need to
write a story, build a presentation, design an experiment, or create a project, but feel
stuck because they cannot think of a strong starting point.
This is one of the best uses of AI in creativity: not replacing the creator, but helping the
creator see more than one path.
Creativity Across Subjects
Students often assume brainstorming belongs only in creative writing or art, but AI-
supported creativity can be useful in many school settings.
Those decisions are what make the final project meaningful.
Asking Better Creative Prompts
Just like in other chapters, better prompts lead to better results.
A weak creative prompt might be:
Give me an idea for a project.

Chapter 11 — AI for Productivity and
Organization
Key Question
How can students use AI to stay organized, manage their time, and complete
schoolwork more effectively?
Why Students Get Overwhelmed
Many students do not struggle because they are lazy or incapable. They struggle because
large tasks are hard to manage when they feel unclear.
A ten-page reading assignment, a science project, or a research paper may seem
manageable to a teacher who has completed many such tasks, but to a student, the same
This does not mean students should follow every AI-generated plan exactly. The point is
to create structure. Once the structure exists, students can adjust it to fit their own
schedule, class requirements, and working style.
Creating Work Plans and Schedules
AI can also be helpful when students are trying to plan their week, manage deadlines, or
A student preparing for a presentation might ask:
Organize these ideas into a three-part presentation structure.
In each case, AI is helping transform scattered material into a clearer format. This can
save time and reduce confusion, especially when students already have the information
but need help making sense of it.
In this example, AI helps Leila get organized, but she still decides how to use the plan
and how much work to complete each day. The AI supports her productivity without
replacing her responsibility.

Part IV — AI Across the Subjects
This part shows what responsible AI use looks like inside real school subjects. Instead of

Chapter 13 — AI in Math
Key Question
How can students use AI to understand mathematical reasoning, practice more
effectively, and learn from mistakes without depending on AI for final answers?
Learning Objectives
Using AI to Understand Steps
Many students get stuck in math not because the entire topic is impossible, but because
one step is unclear. AI can be helpful when students need a process explained more
carefully.
For example, a student might ask:
What is one common mistake students make on this kind of problem?
This is a strong use of AI because students often learn more from corrected mistakes
than from finished solutions. The student is still involved in the math. The tool is simply
helping reveal what needs more attention.
What AI Should Not Replace in Math
Student Example: Learning From the Second Try
A student named Marcus is learning systems of equations. He understands the general
idea, but one homework problem keeps going wrong. Instead of asking for the answer
immediately, he asks AI:
Show me how to solve this system step by step and explain why substitution
Chapter Summary
In this chapter, you learned that AI can support math by explaining steps, generating
practice, and helping students learn from mistakes. You also learned that math
understanding depends on reasoning, not just answers. AI is most useful in math when
it strengthens practice and explanation rather than replacing the work of solving.
Chapter 14 — AI in History and Social Studies
Key Question
How can students use AI to explore history and social studies more deeply while still
thinking critically, checking sources, and understanding multiple perspectives?
Learning Objectives
Using AI to Build Background Knowledge
One of the best uses of AI in history is at the beginning of a topic. Students often need
a quick overview before they are ready to study details more closely.
For example, a student beginning a unit on the Industrial Revolution might ask:
Give me an overview of the Industrial Revolution and explain why it changed
Compare how factory owners and workers experienced the Industrial Revolution.
These questions encourage deeper thinking because they move students beyond a single
viewpoint. They also help students prepare for discussions, essays, and document-based
questions where multiple perspectives matter.
AI and Historical Simulations
Using AI Responsibly in History and Social Studies
In history and social studies, responsible use means treating AI as a tool for inquiry
rather than as evidence. AI can help students organize events, compare viewpoints, or
clarify a topic, but the student still has to check dates, confirm claims, and ask what
perspective may be missing. The more a task depends on evidence and source

Chapter 15 — AI in Science
Key Question
How can students use AI to understand scientific ideas, ask better questions, and
strengthen lab and class learning while still relying on evidence and scientific reasoning?
Learning Objectives
AI for Explaining Difficult Concepts
One of the best uses of AI in science is asking it to explain ideas more clearly. A student
who does not fully understand osmosis, Newton’s laws, chemical bonding, or the rock
cycle may benefit from a simpler explanation or an analogy. A biology student, for
example, might ask for photosynthesis to be explained in simple terms with an everyday
AI and Scientific Questions
AI can also help students ask better science questions.
Science learning becomes stronger when students are curious about how and why things
happen. AI can support that curiosity by generating follow-up questions, possible
hypotheses, or review prompts.

She asks AI:

In this chapter, you learned that AI can support science by clarifying concepts,
comparing vocabulary, generating questions, and helping students review more actively.
You also learned that science depends on evidence, accuracy, and safe procedures, so AI
should support scientific learning rather than replace observation, data, or teacher
Chapter 16 — AI in PE, Health, and Personal
Wellness
Key Question
How can students use AI to support fitness, health learning, goal setting, and personal
wellness in safe, thoughtful ways without replacing professional or teacher guidance?
AI for Understanding Health and Fitness Concepts
For example, a student might ask:
Explain the difference between aerobic and anaerobic exercise in simple terms.
Or:
What are the main benefits of sleep for learning and physical recovery?
Privacy and Personal Boundaries
Students must be especially careful about privacy in this subject area.
They should avoid entering sensitive personal information into AI tools, including:
 private health details
 mental health crises or emergency concerns
Irresponsible uses include:
 sharing private health information
 using AI instead of trusted adults for serious concerns
 following unverified fitness or nutrition advice blindly
 treating AI as a doctor, therapist, or emergency response tool

Part V — Responsible and Future-Ready AI Use
This part looks beyond classroom tasks and focuses on the bigger responsibilities that
come with using AI well. It connects ethics, integrity, future readiness, and long-term
learning habits so students can use AI with judgment and confidence.
Chapter 17 — Using AI Responsibly
Key Question
What does it mean for students to use artificial intelligence responsibly, ethically, and
honestly in school?
Learning Objectives
Responsibility Begins With Purpose
The first question students should ask when using AI is simple:
Why am I using this tool?
That question matters because the same AI feature can be used responsibly in one
situation and irresponsibly in another.
Academic Integrity and AI
Schools have always expected students to do their own work honestly.
That expectation does not disappear just because new technology exists.
Academic integrity means being truthful about what work is yours, what ideas came
from others, and what kind of help you used. In the past, that meant not copying from
Verifying AI-Generated Information
Responsibility also includes checking whether AI responses are accurate.
As you learned earlier in the book, AI systems can generate incorrect information that
sounds polished and believable. This can include false facts, made-up details, inaccurate
summaries, and invented sources.
When a topic has multiple perspectives, responsible AI use means asking broader
questions, comparing responses, and checking additional sources rather than accepting
one answer too quickly.
This is another reason human judgment matters so much. AI can help students explore
ideas, but students must still evaluate fairness, accuracy, and perspective.
Using AI to Strengthen Learning
The most responsible use of AI is the kind that clearly strengthens learning.
Students are usually on solid ground when they use AI to:
 ask for clearer explanations
 generate practice questions
Classroom Idea
Teachers can use this chapter to lead a discussion about what responsible AI use looks
like in real classroom situations.
For example, students can be given sample scenarios and asked to decide whether each
one reflects responsible or irresponsible use.

Chapter 18 — AI, Media Literacy, and What to
Trust
Key Question
How can students tell what to trust in a world where AI can generate realistic text,
images, audio, and video that may be misleading or false?
What AI-Generated Misinformation Looks Like
Misinformation is false or misleading information that spreads as if it were true.
Sometimes it is shared by people who do not realize it is wrong. Other times it is created
or reshaped on purpose to influence, confuse, embarrass, or manipulate others.
AI makes misinformation easier to produce because it can generate believable content
False Summaries and Confident Errors
Not all AI misinformation looks dramatic. Some of it looks ordinary and helpful.
A student might read an AI-generated summary of an article, video, or event and assume
it captures the truth. But summaries can be misleading when they leave out context,
flatten disagreement, exaggerate one point, or quietly include incorrect details. This is
locate, interpret, and evaluate media in a world shaped by deepfakes and
misinformation.
Useful verification habits include:
 cross-checking a claim with trusted news or educational sources
 using reverse-image search when a photo feels suspicious or appears out of
Classroom Idea
Teachers can show students a mix of media examples such as a real news image, an AI-
generated image, a misleading caption, and a short summary of a current event. Students
can work in groups to decide what questions they would ask before trusting or sharing
each one.

Chapter 19 — AI and the Future of Work
Key Question
How is artificial intelligence changing jobs, careers, and the skills students will need in
the future?
Learning Objectives
AI Is Changing Work, Not Ending Work
One of the biggest misunderstandings about AI is the belief that it will simply “take all
the jobs.”
The truth is more complicated.
AI is changing how work gets done, especially in jobs that involve repetitive tasks, large
The Skills That Will Matter More
As AI becomes more capable, some human skills become even more important.
Students often assume that if AI can generate writing, solve problems, or answer
questions, then human thinking matters less. In reality, the opposite is often true.
When information becomes easier to generate, it becomes more important to evaluate,
The goal is not to become dependent on AI. The goal is to become capable in a world
where AI is part of daily work.
AI Will Affect Different Careers in Different Ways
Not every career will be changed in exactly the same way.
Some jobs may rely heavily on AI tools for efficiency. Others may use AI only

A student named Jada enjoys both art and technology but is unsure how those interests
could connect in a future career.
She asks AI:
What careers combine creativity and technology?

Chapter 21 — Becoming an AI-Empowered
Learner
Key Question
How can students use artificial intelligence in ways that strengthen learning, curiosity,
and future readiness?
Curiosity Still Matters Most
One of the greatest mistakes students can make is thinking that AI replaces the need for
curiosity.
In reality, curiosity becomes even more important in the age of AI.
AI can generate answers quickly, but it does not decide which questions matter most. It
AI Should Strengthen Independence, Not Weaken It
There is a difference between getting help and becoming dependent.
A student who uses AI to understand a concept, organize a project, or practice a skill is
using the technology in a way that strengthens independence. Over time, that student
should become more confident, more capable, and more prepared to do similar work on
Those habits matter in school, but they matter just as much in adult life.
Student Example

At first, she used it to explain science concepts and generate quiz questions. Over time,
she became more comfortable asking follow-up questions, checking explanations against
As you continue using AI, challenge yourself to use it in ways that make you more
thoughtful, not less.
Try to be the kind of student who:
 asks better questions
 looks for understanding, not just speed

Why This Chapter Matters
This chapter matters because it brings the book’s main message into focus.
AI is powerful. It can support learning in remarkable ways. But the real difference will
always come from how students choose to use it.
Students who use AI only for quick answers may gain convenience.
Appendix A — Using AI to Build With AI
Purpose of This Appendix
This appendix shows students how to use AI for a different kind of work: not just
answering questions, but helping plan, design, build, test, and improve a project. The
goal is to introduce a practical workflow for using AI across multiple stages of creation
A Student-Friendly Example Project
To make this process concrete, this appendix uses a simple sample project: an AI Study
Quiz Generator. The idea is straightforward. A student enters a topic they want to
review, and the project displays a small set of quiz questions for practice.
This kind of project works well as an example because it connects directly to the rest of
The Builder
This role helps generate the first workable version of the project. Depending on the
task, that might mean writing code, drafting text, creating a checklist, building slides, or
producing a rough prototype.
The Tester and Reviewer
Step 4 — Build a First Draft or Prototype
Once the structure is clear, AI can help generate the first version. If the project involves
code, this may be starter code. If it involves a presentation or plan, it may be a draft
outline or rough content. The goal at this stage is not perfection. The goal is to create
something workable that can be improved.
Common Mistakes to Avoid
 Trying to build something too large before the simple version works
 Accepting AI output without checking whether it matches the goal
 Letting AI make all the design decisions without student judgment
 Using code or project content that the student does not understand
Recommended AI Tools for Students
Artificial intelligence tools are becoming part of everyday learning. Students can now use
AI to ask questions, study for tests, organize ideas, improve writing, generate images,
practice coding, and explore possible careers. But not every AI tool does the same thing
well. Some are strongest at conversation and explanation, while others are better for
AI Chat Assistants
AI chat assistants are the tools most students will recognize first.
These systems allow students to ask questions in conversational language and receive
responses that feel more like dialogue than a search engine result. They are often useful
for explanation, brainstorming, summarizing, studying, and practicing follow-up
At the same time, students should remember that ChatGPT can make mistakes.
Important information should still be checked against class materials, teacher guidance,
or trusted sources.
Claude
Claude is another AI chat assistant that many students find useful for explanation,
 create outlines for essays or presentations
 summarize written material
 support planning and note organization
 assist with data-heavy school tasks
It is especially practical for students who already rely on Microsoft applications for their
AI Research Tools
Research tools are different from chat assistants because they are more focused on
helping users locate, organize, and verify information.
These tools can be especially useful when students are:
 starting a research paper
Elicit
Elicit is more research-oriented and may be especially useful for students or advanced
learners who want help finding academic-style information or summarizing research
sources. It is less of a general chat assistant and more of a research helper.
Students may use Elicit to:
AI Writing Tools
Some AI tools are designed specifically to help with writing, editing, and organization.
These tools are often best used after a student has already started writing. They can
help improve clarity, grammar, structure, and tone, but they should not replace the
student’s own ideas and voice.
AI Image and Design Tools
Some AI tools are especially helpful for visual work.
These tools can support:
 school presentations
 posters
Canva AI
Canva is especially useful because it combines design tools with AI-assisted features.
Students can use it to create polished presentations, posters, reports, or infographics.
This makes Canva especially practical for school because it supports both creativity and
communication.
Used poorly, however, it can make students overdependent. That is why it should be
treated as a coach, not as a replacement for understanding.
Choosing the Right Tool
One of the most important AI skills students can develop is learning how to choose the
right tool for the task.
Classroom Idea
Teachers can use this section to help students compare AI tool categories rather than
focusing only on brand names.
For example, a class might discuss:
 Which tool is best for studying?
